description: Functions that create graphics: line, scatter, bar, statistical and polar plots in two dimensions; contour, surface, mesh, volume and vector-field visualizations in three; image display; function plotting from handles; and the low-level primitives (line, patch, text) that all higher-level charts are built from.

tools.name: plot
tools.description: Creates 2-D line plots of Y against X, drawing one line per column when the inputs are matrices. Line style, marker and colour are set with a short LineSpec string or with name-value pairs, and multiple x-y pairs can be plotted in one call. It is the most used graphics function in MATLAB and returns Line objects you can modify afterwards.
tools.usage:
plot(Y)
plot(X, Y)
plot(X, Y, LineSpec)
plot(X1, Y1, ..., Xn, Yn)
plot(ax, ___)
h = plot(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: X, Y
parameters.description: Data; matrices plot one line per column, and datetime or duration axes are supported.

parameters.name: LineSpec
parameters.description: Combined style, marker and colour such as '-r', '--o', ':k'.

tools.notes: Each call replaces the current axes content unless `hold on` is active. Plotting a matrix plots columns as separate lines, so transpose if your observations are in rows. Very large data sets plot faster when downsampled or drawn with a single NaN-separated line.

tools.name: plot3
tools.description: Plots lines and markers in three dimensions from x, y and z coordinate vectors. Use it for trajectories, parametric space curves and phase portraits of three-state systems. It shares LineSpec and property syntax with `plot`, and the view can be rotated with `view` or the mouse.
tools.usage:
plot3(X, Y, Z)
plot3(X, Y, Z, LineSpec)
plot3(X1, Y1, Z1, ..., Xn, Yn, Zn)
h = plot3(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: X, Y, Z
parameters.description: Coordinate vectors or matrices; matrices plot one line per column.

tools.example:
t = linspace(0, 10*pi, 1000);
plot3(sin(t), cos(t), t, 'LineWidth', 1.2)
grid on
xlabel('x'); ylabel('y'); zlabel('t')
view(45, 25)
tools.notes: For a coloured trajectory where the colour encodes a fourth variable, use `scatter3` or a `patch` with the 'FaceVertexCData' property, since plot3 gives each line a single colour.

tools.name: scatter
tools.description: Draws a scatter plot of discrete points whose size and colour can each vary with the data, producing bubble and colour-coded charts. Use it for correlation plots, for visualizing clusters and for encoding extra variables in marker size and colour. Marker transparency helps with overplotting in dense data.
tools.usage:
scatter(x, y)
scatter(x, y, sz)
scatter(x, y, sz, c)
scatter(___, 'filled')
h = scatter(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: sz
parameters.description: Marker area in points squared; scalar or one per point.

parameters.name: c
parameters.description: Colour: an RGB triplet, a colour name, or a vector mapped through the colormap.

tools.notes: When colour is a numeric vector it maps through the colormap and colour limits; pass an RGB triplet to get one fixed colour. For very large data sets, `scatter` with many markers is slow, so consider `histogram2` or `binscatter`.

tools.name: scatter3
tools.description: Draws a 3-D scatter plot with per-point size and colour control. Use it to visualize point clouds, clustered data in three features, and trajectories where a fourth variable is encoded as colour. Rotate the view to judge structure, and consider transparency for dense clouds.
tools.usage:
scatter3(x, y, z)
scatter3(x, y, z, sz)
scatter3(x, y, z, sz, c)
scatter3(___, 'filled')
h = scatter3(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: sz
parameters.description: Marker area, scalar or per point.

parameters.name: c
parameters.description: Colour data mapped through the colormap, or an RGB triplet.

tools.notes: A 3-D scatter is often harder to read than two 2-D projections; rotate or animate with `view` to convey depth. `plot3` with a marker LineSpec is faster when all points share a colour and size.

tools.name: bar
tools.description: Draws vertical bar charts, grouping or stacking the columns of a matrix. Categorical x data produces one bar per category with automatic tick labels. Use it for counts, comparisons across categories and simple summaries, and set FaceColor per bar with the CData property.
tools.usage:
bar(y)
bar(x, y)
bar(___, width)
bar(___, style)
b = bar(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Bar positions or a categorical array of labels.

parameters.name: y
parameters.description: Bar heights; a matrix produces grouped or stacked bars.

parameters.name: 'FaceColor', 'EdgeColor'
parameters.description: Colours; 'flat' uses the CData property per bar.

tools.notes: Reordering categorical bars requires `reordercats` on the category array, because bars are drawn in category order. `barh` produces horizontal bars with the same options.

tools.name: barh
tools.description: Draws horizontal bar charts, which are easier to read when category names are long. It supports the same grouped and stacked styles as `bar`. Use it for ranked lists, survey results and anything with many textual categories.
tools.usage:
barh(y)
barh(x, y)
barh(___, style)
b = barh(___, Name, Value)
tools.notes: Sorting the data before plotting makes ranked bar charts far more readable. The first category appears at the bottom of the axes by default; use `set(gca,'YDir','reverse')` to flip it.

tools.name: histogram
tools.description: Plots a histogram of data with automatic bin selection, and returns a Histogram object whose BinEdges, BinWidth, Values and Normalization can be adjusted after creation. Use it to inspect distributions, compare groups with transparency, and produce probability or density estimates. It accepts numeric, datetime, duration and categorical data.
tools.usage:
histogram(X)
histogram(X, nbins)
histogram(X, edges)
histogram(___, Name, Value)
h = histogram(___)
tools.notes: Overlaying two histograms without reducing FaceAlpha hides the first one. `histcounts` computes the same bins without plotting, and `histogram2` handles bivariate data.

tools.name: histogram2
tools.description: Plots a bivariate histogram as 3-D bars or as a colour-coded tile map, binning two variables jointly. Use it to visualize the joint distribution of two variables and to reveal structure that overlapping scatter markers obscure. Display styles include 'bar3' and 'tile'.
tools.usage:
histogram2(X, Y)
histogram2(X, Y, nbins)
histogram2(X, Y, Xedges, Yedges)
histogram2(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: Xedges, Yedges
parameters.description: Explicit bin edges in each direction.

tools.notes: The 'tile' style with a colorbar is usually clearer than 3-D bars for dense data. `binscatter` is an alternative that adapts bin sizes automatically for very large data sets.

tools.name: pie
tools.description: Draws a pie chart of the relative sizes of the elements of a vector, optionally exploding selected slices and labelling them. When the data sums to less than 1 it draws a partial pie, which is a common surprise. Use it sparingly, since bar charts are usually easier to compare.
tools.usage:
pie(X)
pie(X, explode)
pie(X, labels)
pie(X, explode, labels)
pie3(___)

parameters.name: explode
parameters.description: Logical or numeric vector marking slices to offset.

parameters.name: labels
parameters.description: Cell array or string array of slice labels.

tools.notes: If sum(X) is less than 1, MATLAB treats the values as fractions and leaves a gap; normalize with `X/sum(X)*1` or pass counts greater than 1. Human perception of angles is poor, so bar charts convey the same data more accurately.

tools.name: area
tools.description: Plots filled areas under curves, stacking the columns of a matrix on top of each other. Use it for cumulative compositions over time, such as resource usage by category or population by group. The BaseValue property sets the baseline, which matters for data that can be negative.
tools.usage:
area(Y)
area(X, Y)
area(___, basevalue)
a = area(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: basevalue
parameters.description: Baseline of the fill; 0 by default.

tools.notes: Stacked areas are hard to read when a lower band varies strongly, because it distorts the ones above; consider separate subplots or a line plot in that case.

tools.name: stairs
tools.description: Draws a stairstep plot, holding each value constant until the next sample. Use it for sampled or piecewise-constant signals, zero-order-hold control outputs and cumulative counts, where a straight interpolating line would misrepresent the data. Output arguments return the expanded x and y vectors without plotting.
tools.usage:
stairs(Y)
stairs(X, Y)
stairs(___, LineSpec)
[xb, yb] = stairs(___)
tools.notes: A discrete control signal drawn with `plot` implies interpolation that did not happen; stairs is the honest representation. `stem` is the alternative when individual samples matter more than the held value.

tools.name: stem
tools.description: Draws a discrete sequence as vertical stems from a baseline with a marker at each data point. Use it for sampled signals, impulse responses and any data where the individual samples, not a continuous curve, are the subject. The 'filled' option and BaseValue property control appearance.
tools.usage:
stem(Y)
stem(X, Y)
stem(___, 'filled')
stem(___, LineSpec)
h = stem(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: 'BaseValue'
parameters.description: Baseline from which stems are drawn.

tools.notes: For long sequences the stems become visual clutter; switch to `plot` or `stairs` above a few hundred points. `stem3` is the three-dimensional version.

tools.name: errorbar
tools.description: Plots data with error bars in one or both directions, either symmetric or with separate negative and positive lengths. Use it to show measurement uncertainty, confidence intervals and standard deviations alongside a mean curve. Cap size and line style are configurable.
tools.usage:
errorbar(y, err)
errorbar(x, y, err)
errorbar(x, y, neg, pos)
errorbar(x, y, yneg, ypos, xneg, xpos)
errorbar(___, LineSpec)
errorbar(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: neg, pos
parameters.description: Separate lower and upper error lengths.

parameters.name: 'CapSize'
parameters.description: Length of the error bar caps in points.

parameters.name: 'vertical'/'horizontal'/'both'
parameters.description: Which direction the bars are drawn in.

tools.notes: Always state in the axis label or caption whether the bars are standard deviations, standard errors or confidence intervals. For shaded confidence bands use `fill` or `patch` with transparency instead.

tools.name: boxchart
tools.description: Draws box plots showing the median, interquartile range, whiskers and outliers of grouped data, with optional secondary grouping by colour. Use it to compare distributions across categories without assuming normality. It is available in core MATLAB since R2020a, unlike the Statistics Toolbox function boxplot.
tools.usage:
boxchart(ydata)
boxchart(xgroupdata, ydata)
boxchart(___, 'GroupByColor', cgroupdata)
b = boxchart(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: xgroupdata
parameters.description: Categorical or numeric grouping along x.

parameters.name: 'GroupByColor'
parameters.description: Second grouping variable drawn in different colours.

tools.notes: Whiskers extend to 1.5 times the interquartile range by default and points beyond are drawn as outliers. Overlay individual observations with `swarmchart` when group sizes are small.

tools.name: swarmchart
tools.description: Draws a swarm chart, a scatter plot in which points within a group are jittered sideways so that none overlap, revealing the full distribution. Use it for small to medium groups where a box plot hides the individual observations. It combines well with `boxchart` drawn on the same axes.
tools.usage:
swarmchart(x, y)
swarmchart(x, y, sz)
swarmchart(x, y, sz, c)
swarmchart(___, Name, Value)
tools.notes: Available since R2020b. For very large groups the swarm becomes a solid block; switch to a violin-style density or a histogram.

tools.name: heatmap
tools.description: Creates a heatmap chart from a matrix or from a table with x, y and colour variables, labelling every cell and optionally displaying the values. It aggregates table data automatically, which makes it a quick pivot-and-visualize tool. Use it for confusion matrices, correlation matrices and category-by-category counts.
tools.usage:
h = heatmap(cdata)
h = heatmap(xvalues, yvalues, cdata)
h = heatmap(tbl, xvar, yvar)
h = heatmap(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: xvalues, yvalues
parameters.description: Labels for the columns and rows.

tools.notes: A heatmap is a chart object, not an axes, so ordinary axes functions like `xlabel` and `hold` do not apply; set its own properties instead. Use `imagesc` when you need a normal axes with full control.

tools.name: polarplot
tools.description: Plots lines in polar coordinates from angle (in radians) and radius vectors, onto polar axes with radial and angular rulers. Use it for antenna patterns, directional data, phase diagrams and anything naturally periodic in angle. The companion `polarscatter` and `polarhistogram` cover points and distributions.
tools.usage:
polarplot(theta, rho)
polarplot(theta, rho, LineSpec)
polarplot(Z)
polarplot(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: Z
parameters.description: Complex values, plotted using angle and magnitude.

tools.notes: Angles are always in radians; use `deg2rad` for degree data. Polar axes have their own properties such as ThetaTick, RLim and ThetaZeroLocation, set on the PolarAxes object rather than through `xlim`/`ylim`.

tools.name: loglog
tools.description: Plots data with logarithmic scaling on both axes, turning power-law relationships into straight lines. Use it for convergence studies, spectra spanning many decades and scaling analyses. Non-positive values cannot be shown and are silently dropped.
tools.usage:
loglog(X, Y)
loglog(X, Y, LineSpec)
loglog(___, Name, Value)
tools.notes: Fitting a line to log10 of the data recovers the power-law exponent, which is the usual reason for a log-log plot. Zeros and negative values vanish without warning, so check your data first.

tools.name: semilogx
tools.description: Plots data with a logarithmic x axis and a linear y axis. Use it for frequency responses, dose-response curves and anything where the independent variable spans decades. It is equivalent to `plot` followed by setting the XScale property to 'log'.
tools.usage:
semilogx(X, Y)
semilogx(X, Y, LineSpec)
semilogx(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: X
parameters.description: Positive values for the logarithmic axis.

tools.notes: `set(gca,'XScale','log')` after a normal plot achieves the same result and works with any plotting function. Minor grid lines help a lot on log axes: `grid minor`.

tools.name: semilogy
tools.description: Plots data with a linear x axis and a logarithmic y axis. Use it for exponential decay and growth, error versus iteration in iterative solvers, and quantities spanning several orders of magnitude. Non-positive y values are dropped.
tools.usage:
semilogy(X, Y)
semilogy(X, Y, LineSpec)
semilogy(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: Y
parameters.description: Positive values for the logarithmic axis.

tools.notes: A straight line on a semilogy plot means exponential behaviour, which is exactly what you look for in convergence plots. Use `loglog` instead when the behaviour is algebraic.

tools.name: fplot
tools.description: Plots a function handle over an interval, choosing sample points adaptively so that sharp features are resolved without manual sampling. Use it for quick visual inspection of mathematical expressions and for functions with steep regions. `fplot3` handles parametric space curves.
tools.usage:
fplot(f)
fplot(f, xinterval)
fplot(funx, funy)
fplot(___, LineSpec)
fp = fplot(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: f
parameters.description: Function handle of one variable; must be vectorized or MeshDensity handled.

parameters.name: 'ShowPoles'
parameters.description: 'on' (default) draws dashed vertical lines at poles.

tools.example:
fplot(@(x) sin(1./x), [0.01 1])
fplot(@(x) tan(x), [-2*pi 2*pi])
ylim([-10 10])
fplot(@(t) sin(t), @(t) cos(3*t), [0 2*pi])
tools.notes: The function handle should be vectorized with elementwise operators; otherwise increase MeshDensity or wrap with `arrayfun`. Adaptive sampling can still miss extremely narrow features.

tools.name: fsurf
tools.description: Plots a surface from a function handle of two variables, or from parametric functions of two parameters, sampling adaptively over the given domain. Use it to visualize mathematical surfaces without building a meshgrid by hand. `fmesh` and `fcontour` are the wireframe and contour counterparts.
tools.usage:
fsurf(f)
fsurf(f, xyinterval)
fsurf(funx, funy, funz)
fsurf(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: xyinterval
parameters.description: [xmin xmax ymin ymax] or a two-element interval used for both.

tools.example:
fsurf(@(x,y) sin(x).*cos(y), [-pi pi -pi pi])
colorbar
fsurf(@(u,v) u.*cos(v), @(u,v) u.*sin(v), @(u,v) u, [0 2 0 2*pi])
axis equal
tools.notes: Increase MeshDensity for smoother surfaces at the cost of rendering time. `fcontour` gives a cheaper 2-D view of the same function.

tools.name: fimplicit
tools.description: Plots the implicit curve f(x,y) = 0 over a region, which is impossible to do with an explicit function plot when the relation cannot be solved for y. Use it for conic sections, level sets and geometric constraints. `fimplicit3` draws implicit surfaces in three dimensions.
tools.usage:
fimplicit(f)
fimplicit(f, interval)
fimplicit(___, LineSpec)
fimplicit(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: f
parameters.description: Function handle f(x,y) whose zero set is drawn.

parameters.name: interval
parameters.description: [xmin xmax ymin ymax] or a two-element interval.

parameters.name: 'MeshDensity'
parameters.description: Sampling density of the underlying grid.

tools.example:
fimplicit(@(x,y) x.^2 + y.^2 - 4, [-3 3])
axis equal
grid on
hold on
fimplicit(@(x,y) x.^2 - y.^2 - 1, [-3 3], '--r')
hold off
fimplicit3(@(x,y,z) x.^2 + y.^2 + z.^2 - 1)
tools.notes: Curves that pass exactly through grid intersections or that have singular points may render with small gaps; raise MeshDensity. A contour at level 0 from `contour` gives similar results with explicit control over the grid.

tools.name: contour
tools.description: Draws contour lines of a matrix of values over a grid, at automatically chosen or explicitly specified levels. Use it for topographic maps, potential fields and any scalar field where level curves convey the structure. With output arguments it returns the contour matrix, which `clabel` uses to label lines.
tools.usage:
contour(Z)
contour(X, Y, Z)
contour(___, levels)
contour(___, LineSpec)
[M, c] = contour(___)

parameters.name: levels
parameters.description: Number of levels, or a vector of level values; [v v] draws a single level.

tools.notes: To draw exactly one contour level v, pass the two-element vector [v v]; a scalar is interpreted as a number of levels. `contourf` fills between levels and `contour3` draws them at their z heights.

tools.name: contourf
tools.description: Draws filled contour plots, colouring the regions between contour levels. Use it when the magnitude of a scalar field matters as much as the level curves, for example in temperature and pressure maps. It shares all the level and labelling options of `contour`.
tools.usage:
contourf(Z)
contourf(X, Y, Z)
contourf(___, levels)
[M, c] = contourf(___)

parameters.name: levels
parameters.description: Number of levels or explicit level vector.

parameters.name: 'LineColor'
parameters.description: Colour of the contour lines; 'none' hides them.

tools.notes: Setting 'LineColor' to 'none' gives a smooth image-like result. For a diverging field, use a diverging colormap and symmetric colour limits with `clim([-m m])`.

tools.name: surf
tools.description: Draws a 3-D shaded surface from a matrix of z values over a grid, with face colours taken from z or from a separate colour matrix. Use it for visualizing functions of two variables, terrain and any gridded scalar field. Shading, lighting and transparency properties control the appearance.
tools.usage:
surf(Z)
surf(X, Y, Z)
surf(X, Y, Z, C)
surf(___, Name, Value)
s = surf(___)
tools.notes: With dense grids the black mesh edges dominate; set EdgeColor to 'none' or use `shading interp`. `surfc` adds a contour plot beneath the surface and `mesh` draws a wireframe.

tools.name: mesh
tools.description: Draws a 3-D wireframe mesh whose lines are coloured by height, with the faces left transparent by default. Use it when the grid structure itself is informative and when you want to see through the surface. `meshc` adds a contour plot underneath and `meshz` adds a curtain around the edges.
tools.usage:
mesh(Z)
mesh(X, Y, Z)
mesh(X, Y, Z, C)
mesh(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: C
parameters.description: Colour data for the mesh lines.

tools.notes: `hidden off` makes the mesh see-through, which helps when the surface folds over itself. For large grids reduce the resolution before plotting to keep interaction responsive.

tools.name: surfc
tools.description: Draws a shaded surface together with a contour plot projected onto the plane below it, combining the height view with level curves. Use it when readers need both the shape and precise level information. It accepts the same arguments and properties as `surf`.
tools.usage:
surfc(Z)
surfc(X, Y, Z)
surfc(X, Y, Z, C)
surfc(___, Name, Value)
tools.notes: The contours are drawn at the bottom of the z limits, so changing `zlim` moves them. Use `meshc` for the wireframe equivalent.

tools.name: meshgrid
tools.description: Creates 2-D or 3-D coordinate grids from coordinate vectors, in the orientation expected by `surf`, `contour`, `quiver` and `interp2`, where x varies along columns. Use it to evaluate a function of two variables on a rectangular grid. `ndgrid` produces the transposed, array-indexing orientation.
tools.usage:
[X, Y] = meshgrid(x, y)
[X, Y] = meshgrid(x)
[X, Y, Z] = meshgrid(x, y, z)
tools.notes: meshgrid returns arrays of size numel(y)-by-numel(x), which is the reverse of what beginners expect. Since R2016b implicit expansion often makes the full grids unnecessary: `Z = x.^2 + (y').^2` computes the same thing without allocating X and Y.

tools.name: ndgrid
tools.description: Creates N-dimensional coordinate grids in array-indexing orientation, where the first input varies along the first dimension. Use it with `interpn`, `griddedInterpolant` and any code that indexes arrays by subscript rather than by plot coordinates. It generalizes to any number of dimensions, unlike `meshgrid`.
tools.usage:
[X1, X2] = ndgrid(x1, x2)
[X1, ..., Xn] = ndgrid(x1, ..., xn)
[X1, ..., Xn] = ndgrid(x)
tools.notes: ndgrid(x,y) and meshgrid(x,y) differ by a transpose for the 2-D case, which is the single most common cause of transposed plots and wrong interpolation results.

tools.name: imagesc
tools.description: Displays a matrix as a colour image, scaling the data to span the full colormap range. Use it to view matrices, correlation structures, spectrograms and gridded fields quickly. Unlike `image`, it does not require the data to be in a particular range.
tools.usage:
imagesc(C)
imagesc(x, y, C)
imagesc(___, clims)
h = imagesc(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: x, y
parameters.description: Two-element vectors giving the coordinate extent of the image.

parameters.name: 'AlphaData'
parameters.description: Per-pixel transparency, useful for masking NaN.

tools.example:
A = peaks(64);
imagesc(A)
axis image
colorbar
colormap(turbo)
imagesc([-3 3], [-3 3], A, [-8 8])
set(gca, 'YDir', 'normal')
tools.notes: The y axis is reversed by default because images are drawn top-down; set YDir to 'normal' for mathematical orientation. NaN values render as the lowest colour unless you set AlphaData to hide them.

tools.name: image
tools.description: Displays image data without rescaling: indexed data maps directly into the colormap and truecolor data is shown as RGB. Use it when the values are already meaningful colour indices or RGB triplets, as with data from `imread`. `imagesc` is the choice when the data is arbitrary numeric values.
tools.usage:
image(C)
image(x, y, C)
h = image(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: C
parameters.description: Indexed image matrix or M-by-N-by-3 truecolor array.

tools.notes: For double indexed data, index 1 is the first colormap entry, so a matrix of zeros displays as the lowest colour clipped. Setting CDataMapping to 'scaled' makes image behave like imagesc.

tools.name: pcolor
tools.description: Draws a pseudocolor checkerboard plot, effectively a flat surface viewed from above, with one coloured cell per grid rectangle. Use it for gridded fields when you want a normal axes with full control over ticks and limits. Note that the last row and column of the data are not displayed in the default faceted mode.
tools.usage:
pcolor(C)
pcolor(X, Y, C)
h = pcolor(___)

parameters.name: X, Y
parameters.description: Grid coordinates, one more than the data cells for exact alignment.

tools.notes: Cell colours come from the value at the lower-left corner, so the final row and column are dropped; pad the data or use `imagesc` to avoid losing them. `shading interp` smooths the cells into a continuous field.

tools.name: quiver
tools.description: Draws a 2-D vector field as arrows at the given positions, automatically scaling them so they do not overlap. Use it for velocity fields, gradients, force fields and flow visualization. Set the scale to 0 to draw arrows at their true length.
tools.usage:
quiver(U, V)
quiver(X, Y, U, V)
quiver(___, scale)
quiver(___, LineSpec)
q = quiver(___, Name, Value)
tools.notes: Automatic scaling makes arrow lengths comparable within one plot but not between plots; pass an explicit scale when comparing. Thin the grid for readability, since a dense field becomes an unreadable mat of arrows.

tools.name: quiver3
tools.description: Draws a 3-D vector field as arrows in space, with the same automatic scaling as `quiver`. Use it for three-dimensional flow fields, surface normals and magnetic or electric field visualization. Combine it with a surface or slice plot to give the arrows context.
tools.usage:
quiver3(X, Y, Z, U, V, W)
quiver3(Z, U, V, W)
quiver3(___, scale)
quiver3(___, LineSpec)
tools.notes: Depth perception in 3-D quiver plots is poor without a reference surface or lighting; add one. `surfnorm` computes surface normals to draw with quiver3.

tools.name: streamline
tools.description: Draws streamlines through a vector field, tracing the paths that massless particles would follow from given starting points. Use it for fluid flow, electromagnetic field lines and any steady vector field where trajectories are more informative than arrows. `stream2` and `stream3` compute the vertex data without drawing.
tools.usage:
streamline(X, Y, U, V, startx, starty)
streamline(X, Y, Z, U, V, W, startx, starty, startz)
streamline(vertices)
h = streamline(___, options)
tools.notes: Streamlines stop when they leave the grid or reach the maximum vertex count, so seed points near the boundary may produce very short lines. `streamslice` picks seed points automatically and is often easier to use.

tools.name: fill
tools.description: Draws filled polygons from vertex coordinates, with a single colour or per-vertex colours interpolated across the face. Use it for shaded confidence bands, highlighted regions and simple shapes. `fill3` does the same in three dimensions.
tools.usage:
fill(X, Y, C)
fill(X, Y, ColorSpec)
fill(X1, Y1, C1, X2, Y2, C2, ...)
h = fill(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: X, Y
parameters.description: Polygon vertex coordinates; columns define separate polygons.

parameters.name: C
parameters.description: Colour: an RGB triplet, a colour letter, or per-vertex values.

tools.notes: The band idiom `[x fliplr(x)]` with `[upper fliplr(lower)]` traces the outline of the region in one closed loop. `patch` offers more control including per-face data and transparency maps.

tools.name: patch
tools.description: Creates one or more filled polygons from explicit vertices and faces, the low-level primitive behind surfaces, filled contours and 3-D meshes. Use it for custom geometry, finite element mesh display, isosurfaces and anything needing per-face or per-vertex colouring. The Faces/Vertices form is the efficient way to draw many polygons sharing vertices.
tools.usage:
patch(X, Y, C)
patch(X, Y, Z, C)
patch('Faces', F, 'Vertices', V, 'FaceColor', c)
patch('XData', x, 'YData', y)
p = patch(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: 'Faces'
parameters.description: Matrix where each row lists the vertex indices of one face.

parameters.name: 'Vertices'
parameters.description: Matrix of vertex coordinates, one row per vertex.

parameters.name: 'FaceVertexCData'
parameters.description: Colour data per face or per vertex.

tools.notes: Faces must list vertices in consistent order; inconsistent winding causes strange lighting. For thousands of polygons, one patch with a Faces/Vertices pair is far faster than many separate patch calls.

tools.name: line
tools.description: Creates a low-level Line object in the current axes without clearing existing content or rescaling the axes. Use it for reference lines, annotations tied to data coordinates and when adding to a plot inside a loop where `hold` management would be awkward. `xline` and `yline` are the convenient constant-line alternatives.
tools.usage:
line(X, Y)
line(X, Y, Z)
line(Name, Value)
line(ax, ___)
h = line(___)
tools.notes: Unlike `plot`, `line` never resets the axes or applies the colour order, so it does not disturb an existing figure. Creating an empty line and updating its XData and YData is the efficient pattern for animation.

tools.name: text
tools.description: Adds text at specified data coordinates, with control over alignment, rotation, font and interpreter. Use it to annotate points, label curves and place values on bars. TeX and LaTeX interpreters allow mathematical notation.
tools.usage:
text(x, y, txt)
text(x, y, z, txt)
text(___, Name, Value)
t = text(___)

parameters.name: txt
parameters.description: Text to display; a cell or string array places one label per position.

parameters.name: 'HorizontalAlignment', 'VerticalAlignment'
parameters.description: Anchoring of the text relative to the point.

tools.example:
x = 1:5; y = [2 5 3 6 4];
plot(x, y, '-o')
text(x, y + 0.2, string(y), 'HorizontalAlignment', 'center')
text(3, 5.5, '$\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx$', 'Interpreter', 'latex', 'FontSize', 14)
tools.notes: Underscores and carets trigger TeX subscript and superscript formatting; set Interpreter to 'none' for literal file names and variable names. `annotation` places text in figure coordinates instead of data coordinates.
